testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: what is vibe testing and why isn't it enough for deploying an llm app?
testCases.actualOutput:
Vibe testing is a very informal way of checking an LLM‑based application. You simply fire off a handful of prompts—usually five or ten—look at the answers, and decide by “feel” whether the system is doing what you want. It’s a quick, ad‑hoc check that relies on your personal impression rather than any systematic metric.

Because it’s based on a handful of random questions, it’s inherently subjective and not repeatable. If you run the same test a month later, you’ll probably ask different questions and get different results, so you can’t guarantee that the behavior you saw once will hold in the future. That lack of repeatability means you can’t reliably document or audit the system’s performance.

In a production setting, you need rigorous, repeatable evaluation: defined test suites, coverage metrics, error rates, and often user studies. Vibe testing doesn’t provide that level of assurance, so deploying an LLM app based solely on it would risk unexpected failures, inconsistent user experience, and a lack of accountability—something the industry simply can’t accept for production‑grade software.

testCases.actualOutput: The MMLU benchmark is a collection of multiple‑choice questions that people use to test how well large language models can answer general knowledge and reasoning questions.  In its original form it covered a wide range of subjects—about 57 different fields—and was a popular yardstick for model performance for a couple of years.  To make it harder, a later version called **MMLU Pro** was introduced.  MMLU Pro kept the same overall goal but tightened the format: each question now has ten answer choices, and the set was trimmed down to 12 subjects with roughly 12 000 questions (about 1 000 per subject).  This made the benchmark more challenging and helped keep it useful as newer models began to surpass the earlier version.  In short, MMLU is a broad, multiple‑choice knowledge test that has evolved into MMLU Pro to stay a relevant benchmark for evaluating language models.

testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: how did mmlu pro improve on the original mmlu?
testCases.actualOutput: MMLU Pro builds on the original MMLU by making the test harder and more focused on genuine reasoning. Instead of the standard four‑choice multiple‑choice format, MMLU Pro gives each question ten possible answers, which forces a model (or a human) to sift through more distractors and eliminates the simple “pick the one you know” strategy. In addition, the creators removed the very basic or noisy items that were common in the original benchmark and replaced them with questions that require deeper reasoning. The result is a set of problems that are more demanding and that better probe a model’s ability to think through a problem rather than just recall facts.
